Well it depends on what class you follow in Ethics.
First, there is consequentialism. These are positions that are concerned by the consequences of your actions more than the actions themselves. If I just brushed my teeth, and am about to drink some orange juice, It's the aftertaste that makes this idea wrong.
Then there is the deontology class, the actions themselves have moral weight, and are judged against a moral norm. The act of drinking that orange juice is wrong in itself, even if there was no aftertaste.
And then finally, there are Virtue Ethics, where the rules aren't about actions or their consequences, but to your character itself. I wouldn't drink that orange juice, because I want to be happy in my life, and drinking that would not contribute to the overall goal.

As a side effect of an upbringing characterised by poverty, violence and the almost constant presence of people with Cluster B personality disorders, I was misdiagnosed as having a developmental disorder. As a condition of being allowed to go to a normal school, I was put in a pilot program where they were doing some experimental psychological treatments to children suspected of having developmental disorders.

That makes it sound unnecessarily spooky, they were trialing Cognitive Behavioural Therapy on children much younger than they normally do. This program ended up getting shelved because it turns out that when you teach young and impressionable people how to rewrite their thought patterns, you essentially give them admin access to their own brains. Most of the time, that goes really badly, because that's too much power for a troubled young kid to use responsibly.

I got out with rather mild side effects, like I went a bit overzealous with purging unpleasant memories and thus have very little conscious recall over my childhood (I am totally OK with that - it sucked).
